content: Mauveine, also referred to as aniline purple or Perkin's mauve, holds the distinction of being the first synthetic organic dye. Its chemical designation is 3-amino-2,±9-dimethyl-5-phenyl-7-(p-tolylamino)phenazinium acetate. The molecular formula for mauveine A is C26H23N4+X−, while mauveine B is represented as C27H25N4+X−. In 1856, William Henry Perkin, an 18-year-old chemist, discovered mauveine by accident while attempting to synthesize quinine, an anti-malarial drug, under the guidance of his professor, August Wilhelm von Hofmann. During one of his experiments, Perkin oxidized aniline using potassium dichromate. The aniline, which contained toluidine impurities, reacted to form a black solid, a common byproduct in unsuccessful organic syntheses. However, while cleaning his flask, Perkin noticed that a portion of the black solid dissolved in alcohol, producing a purple solution. This solution turned out to be an effective dye for silk and other textiles. Perkin patented the dye and, in 1857, established a factory in Greenford, London, along the Grand Union Canal to produce it on a large scale. Initially marketed as aniline purple or Tyrian purple (a name derived from a natural dye obtained from mollusks), the dye was later named mauve in England in 1859, inspired by the French word malva, referring to the mallow flower. Chemists subsequently adopted the term mauveine. Mauve became a highly fashionable color in 1862 when Queen Victoria wore a mauve silk gown at the Royal Exhibition. Although its popularity waned by the late 1860s due to the emergence of newer synthetic dyes, mauveine had already secured Perkin's financial success and laid the foundation for the synthetic chemical industry. By the early 20th century, the U.S. National Association of Confectioners approved mauveine as a food coloring under various names, including rosolan, violet paste, chrome violet, anilin violet, Perkins violet, indisin, phenamin, purpurin, tyralin, Tyrian purple, and lydin. Furthermore, advancements in chemical dye research, partly inspired by mauveine, contributed to the development of modern chemotherapy, such as sulfonamide drugs. The dye's distinctive color was also widely recognized due to its use in spirit duplicator printing machines, commonly known by the trade name Ditto, during the mid-20th century. The modern synthesis of mauveine involves dissolving a mixture of aniline, p-toluidine, and o-toluidine in sulfuric acid and water in a 1:1:2 ratio, followed by the addition of potassium dichromate. Determining the precise molecular structure of mauveine proved challenging and was not definitively resolved until 1994. Mauveine is, in fact, a mixture of four closely related aromatic compounds that differ in the number and arrangement of methyl groups. Mauveine A is composed of two molecules of aniline, one molecule of p-toluidine, and one molecule of o-toluidine. Mauveine B, on the other hand, consists of one molecule each of aniline, p-toluidine, and o-toluidine. In 1879, Perkin demonstrated that mauveine B is chemically related to safranines, as it can undergo oxidative or reductive loss of the p-tolyl group. Safranine itself is a 2,8-dimethyl phenazinium salt, while parasafranine, as produced by Perkin, is presumed to be the 1,8or 2,9-dimethyl isomer. In 2007, two additional components of mauveine were identified. Mauveine C contains an extra p-methyl group compared to mauveine A, while mauveine B2 is an isomer of mauveine B, differing in the placement of the methyl group on the aryl ring.
